blocks.content: Chapter 8: Force and Laws of Motion
8.1 Balanced and Unbalanced Forces

A force can be a push or a pull. When several forces act on a body at the same time, their effects can cancel one another. Such forces are called balanced forces. If the net force on an object is not zero, the forces are unbalanced and the object accelerates in the direction of the net force.

Consider a wooden block resting on a table. The weight of the block acts downwards and the table pushes upwards with an equal force. These two forces are balanced, so the block stays at rest. Now imagine pushing the block sideways. If the applied force is greater than the force of friction, the block begins to move. The forces are now unbalanced.
An unbalanced force is needed to change the state of motion of an object. It can change the speed of the object, the direction of its motion, or both.
8.2 First Law of Motion
An object remains in a state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force. This is Newton's first law of motion, also called the law of inertia.

Inertia is the natural tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of motion. The mass of an object is a measure of its inertia. A heavier object has greater inertia than a lighter one, so a larger force is needed to change its state of motion.

Everyday observations illustrate this law. When a moving bus brakes suddenly, passengers lean forward because their bodies continue to move even though the bus has slowed. When the bus starts suddenly, passengers fall backwards, because their bodies were at rest and tend to remain at rest.
8.3 Second Law of Motion
The rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied unbalanced force in the direction of the force.
Momentum is the product of the mass and the velocity of an object.
p = m * v
The second law can be written in the familiar form:
F = m * a

where F is the force applied, m is the mass of the object, and a is the acceleration produced. The SI unit of force is the newton (N). One newton is the force that produces an acceleration of 1 metre per second squared in an object of mass 1 kilogram.
Example 8.1: A force of 5 N acts on a mass of 2 kg. The acceleration produced is a = F/m = 5/2 = 2.5 metre per second squared.

Example 8.2: A cricket player pulls his hands backwards while catching a fast ball. By doing so he increases the time taken to reduce the momentum of the ball to zero. Since the rate of change of momentum is reduced, the force exerted on his hands is smaller and injury is avoided.
8.4 Third Law of Motion
To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. These forces always act on two different bodies, never on the same body.

When a bullet is fired from a gun, the gun exerts a forward force on the bullet and the bullet exerts an equal backward force on the gun. This is why the gun recoils. Because the mass of the gun is much larger than that of the bullet, the acceleration of the gun is much smaller.
A person walking pushes backwards on the ground, and the ground pushes the person forward with an equal force. Without this reaction force, walking would not be possible.
8.5 Conservation of Momentum

When two objects collide, the total momentum of the two objects before the collision is equal to the total momentum after the collision, provided no external unbalanced force acts on them. This is the law of conservation of momentum.

| Law | Statement | Key idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | An object keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts | Inertia |
| Second | Rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force | F equals m times a |
| Third | Action and reaction are equal and opposite | Forces act on two bodies |

## 8.3 Second Law of Motion

p = m * v
